column1: In standard CNC Cartesian convention, which direction is positive Z and what does negative Z motion accomplish?
column2: Positive Z points away from the spindle toward the operator; negative Z motion plunges the tool into the workpiece.

column1: Using the right-hand rule for CNC rotational axes, which linear axis does each rotational axis (A, B, C) correspond to?
column2: A rotates about X, B rotates about Y, C rotates about Z.

column1: How do you calculate linear table displacement per motor revolution on a ballscrew-driven axis?
column2: Displacement equals the ballscrew's lead (pitch); e.g., a 5mm-pitch ballscrew advances the table 5mm per motor revolution, creating a deterministic ratio between encoder counts and position.

column1: What is the difference between G01 and G00 in G-code, and why does their modal nature matter?
column2: G01 is linear interpolation at a programmed feedrate; G00 is rapid traverse. Both are modal—they persist across subsequent blocks until explicitly superseded—so an inherited modal state from a prior operation can silently alter subsequent motion if not managed.

column1: What is the purpose of G54–G59 (and extended G54.1 P1-P99) work coordinate offsets?
column2: They establish floating coordinate systems aligned to workpiece features (corner edges, bore centers, datum surfaces) rather than requiring programming in raw machine coordinates.

column1: Define rake angle and explain the tradeoff between positive and negative rake.
column2: Rake angle is the inclination of the cutting face from a plane perpendicular to the cutting velocity vector. Positive rake sharpens the edge, lowers cutting forces, but thins the wedge (more prone to chipping/shock) — used for soft/gummy materials like aluminum (+15° to +20°). Negative/neutral rake thickens the wedge for strength, used for hardened steel/Inconel roughing.

column1: What happens if a cutting tool's relief (clearance) angle is zero?
column2: The tool rubs against the freshly machined surface instead of cutting, generating heat and wear without effective material removal.

column1: Explain the 3-2-1 locating principle for workholding and how it constrains the six degrees of freedom.
column2: A primary datum plane uses 3 contact points to eliminate 1 translational + 2 rotational DOF; a secondary datum uses 2 points to eliminate 1 translational + 1 rotational DOF; a tertiary datum uses 1 point to eliminate the final translational DOF — fully constraining all 6 DOF with minimum contact.

column1: Why does over-constraining a workpiece (using 4+ contact points on a datum plane) cause problems?
column2: A fourth point on an imperfect real surface creates a kinematically indeterminate contact that rocks unpredictably under clamping force, leading to part distortion.

column1: What are the six degrees of freedom that a complete workholding setup must constrain?
column2: Three translational (X, Y, Z) and three rotational (rotation about each of the three axes).

column1: What is the first physical action that must be performed before beginning any CNC verification lab exercise, and why?
column2: Tramming the vise (sweeping the fixed jaw with a dial test indicator along its travel and adjusting until aligned), because every downstream dimensional result depends on a properly trammed, rigid workholding reference.

column1: According to RS-274D, into how many modal groups are G-code commands standardized, and what categories do they govern?
column2: Fourteen modal groups, governing motion type, coordinate systems, feedrate modes, cutter compensation, and coolant state, among others.
